knownFor: Teacher and Bible scholar at Alexandria and Caesarea, who wrote commentaries on Scripture and a book of doctrine that was argued over for centuries.

keyWorks.about: the Hebrew text set beside the Greek translations; the church historian Eusebius of Caesarea says Origen left us copies of it. Jerome says Origen searched out three more translations, which Jerome himself had from Origen's library

traces: Eusebius of Caesarea tells of two brothers, Gregory the Wonderworker and Athenodorus, who came to Origen at Caesarea full of zeal for Greek and Roman learning. He gave them a love of philosophy and turned them to the study of divinity. After five years with him, both became bishops in Pontus.
A letter Origen wrote to that Gregory survives in the Philocalia. It urges him to take from Greek learning whatever serves Christianity, as geometry and grammar serve philosophy.
Gregory of Nazianzus, sending the Philocalia to a friend, called it a selection of passages useful to students of literature.
remembered: The church historian Socrates of Constantinople, who defended Origen, names four men who attacked him: Methodius of Olympus, Eustathius of Antioch, Apollinaris and Theophilus of Alexandria. He says each blamed a different point, and none charged Origen with unsound teaching on the Trinity.
Socrates of Constantinople also says Theophilus of Alexandria wrote to the bishops condemning Origen's books, to hide his real aim, which was to move against John Chrysostom.
Epiphanius of Cyprus charged, and Jerome repeated, that Origen taught even the devil would one day repent.

The Fifth Council at Constantinople, in 553, named Origen in its eleventh anathema, beside Arius and others. The historian Evagrius Scholasticus says the council also issued special anathemas against him. Whether it did is still disputed. Hefele reports that Halloix, Garnier, Basnage, Walch and others held Origen's name to be a later insertion in that anathema. He rejects this, because the copy of the acts in the Roman archives has the name.

uncertain: We read On First Principles mostly in Rufinus of Aquileia's Latin, and Jerome said Rufinus changed it. Rufinus says in his preface: "we have either left them out as passages which had been falsified or inserted, or else have changed the expression in accordance with the rule of faith."

Jerome says Origen was ordained in Palestine on a journey, which so enraged his bishop Demetrius that he wrote everywhere to ruin Origen's name. Eusebius of Caesarea orders it differently: Demetrius wrote against Origen first, out of jealousy, and the ordination came after.

Eusebius of Caesarea is our witness that Origen took a saying of Jesus too literally and made himself a eunuch. He adds that Demetrius at first admired the act, then wrote of it to bishops everywhere as most foolish. Jerome says only that Demetrius was wildly enraged at Origen after his ordination.
Eusebius of Caesarea says Origen died in the time of the emperor Trebonianus Gallus, at sixty-nine. Jerome adds that he died at Tyre and was buried there.

briefReferences: Eusebius, Church History VI.1-2, tr. A. C. McGiffert: Severus's persecution, believers of Egypt brought to Alexandria, many dying, Origen's father among those arrested. The year 202 is the edition's reckoning from Eusebius's "tenth year" of Severus.
Eusebius, Church History VI.2.3-6, tr. McGiffert: Origen's longing for martyrdom, his mother hiding his clothes, the letter to his father: "Take heed not to change your mind on our account."
Eusebius, Church History VI.2.12-13, tr. McGiffert: his father's death as a martyr.
Eusebius, Church History VI.3, tr. McGiffert: in his eighteenth year he took charge of teaching, because the others were driven away.
Eusebius, Church History VI.26, tr. McGiffert: his move to Caesarea. The year 231 is the edition's reckoning from the tenth year of Alexander.
Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 54, tr. Ernest Cushing Richardson: he learned Hebrew against the habit of his time; he died at Tyre.
Eusebius, Church History VI.16, tr. McGiffert: the Hebrew text set beside the Greek versions, the Hexapla.
Jerome, Preface to Job, tr. W. H. Fremantle: Origen's marks where the old Greek fell short; Jerome defending his Latin Job against critics by those marks.
Origen, On First Principles IV, tr. Frederick Crombie (Rufinus's Latin): Scripture has body, soul and spirit; the plain story for simple believers, the deeper senses for those who have gone further.
Origen, Philocalia, chapters I-XIV, tr. George Lewis: the book of passages chosen from him opens with chapters on how Scripture should be read.
Athanasius, On the Decrees of the Council of Nicaea 27, ed. Archibald Robertson: the Son always with the Father; Athanasius, defending Nicaea, calls on "the labour-loving Origen" as a witness.
Eusebius, Church History VI.30, tr. McGiffert: Gregory and Athenodorus, who came to him for Greek learning, both became bishops in Pontus.
Eusebius, Church History VI.39.5, tr. McGiffert: in the persecution under Decius, his bonds and bodily tortures, his feet stretched in the stocks for many days.
Origen, On First Principles, tr. Crombie (Rufinus's Latin): souls before bodies. Rufinus's Latin is the only form in which we read it, and Rufinus says he changed passages.
Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 83, tr. Richardson: Methodius wrote On the Resurrection against Origen.
Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 75, tr. Richardson: Pamphilus of Caesarea's defense of Origen. Eusebius, Church History VI.23, tr. McGiffert: "the Defense which we have composed in his behalf".
Fifth Council (Constantinople, 553), Anathema XI, tr. Henry R. Percival: Origen named among those condemned.
